parts.note: a cham is an old word for a khan or despot, as in Johnson's nickname 'the great Cham'

explanation.surface: A tutor at court behaving like a dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Ascham was tutor to the young Elizabeth I. CHAM, an archaic form of khan, means an autocrat.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Ascham taught Greek and Latin to Princess Elizabeth, later Queen Elizabeth I.

definitions.meaning: John ..., the Tudor and Stuart cartographer of English counties
taken in the sense of quickness rather than a stronghold

explanation.definitionFit: John Speed drew famous county maps around 1610, and rapidity or swiftness is another word for fastness.

clue.text: She makes the case for a sewer

definitions.text: She makes the case for a sewer

parts.words: She makes the case for a sewer
parts.note: reads like a woman arguing in favour of a drain, but describes both a homemaker and a small sewing kit holding needles and thread

explanation.surface: A woman argues the merits of a drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sewer' is one who sews, not a drain; the same word names a pocket needlecase, traditionally pronounced 'hussif'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a woman running a home and a small case of sewing materials.

parts.note: an ape's name joins 'business' for mischief, and the same word is slang for five hundred pounds

explanation.surface: Asking whether some shady deal turns a profit of 500.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a 'monkey' is £500, and 'monkey business' is underhand dealing.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for five hundred pounds, and the first word of the idiom for trickery.

definitions.meaning: held in one's arms, wrapped around
cryptically, put into a fold as sheep are penned

explanation.definitionFit: To wrap up or hug, and also literally to pen inside a fold, the enclosure for sheep.

clue.text: Author is angry with new theme being changed

indicators.note: the letters of the words beside it are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A writer cross that a fresh theme is being altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being changed' signals an anagram of IS ANGRY plus NEW THEME; 'with' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist who wrote The Old Man and the Sea.

definitions.meaning: literally the nip a parasitic insect gives

explanation.definitionFit: A tiny inconvenience, and literally the bite of a small jumping parasite.

definitions.meaning: the scales, which this constellation represents

explanation.definitionFit: The seventh zodiac sign, symbolised by a pair of scales.

clue.text: Shoots along the line if fed saline compound

indicators.note: a compound is a mixture, so these letters are blended into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Giving salt water to something along a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compound' signals an anagram of FED plus SALINE; 'if' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To enfilade is to rake a line of troops with gunfire from end to end.

clue.text: Aversion to purge mixed by girl

indicators.note: mixed means the letters of purge are jumbled together

parts.note: Nance is a girl's name, a pet form of Anne

explanation.surface: A girl's dislike of taking a laxative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' scrambles the laxative's letters; Nance is an old pet form of Anne, a stock crossword girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Repugnance is strong distaste or loathing.

definitions.meaning: to shine or rub up a surface

explanation.definitionFit: To shine a surface, an enthusiast, and the dull yellow leather made from hide.

indicators.note: drop-out tells us the named part is dropped out of the longer name

parts.note: love-in-idleness is an old country name for the wild pansy
taken as written, a hippie gathering

explanation.surface: A hippie drop-out at a love-in, doing nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The pansy's folk name LOVE-IN-IDLENESS loses LOVE-IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inactive is the state of having nothing doing.

clue.text: Bumble bee has tormented lad kept in

indicators.note: kept in means one piece is held inside the other
tormented means the word lad is twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A bee keeping a teased boy shut in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bumble' looks like the bee's buzzing, but is Dickens's parish official; 'tormented' scrambles the boy and 'kept in' holds him inside the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Bumble is the pompous parish officer in Dickens's Oliver Twist.

indicators.note: endless means the final letter is cut off the word

parts.note: a topic is something talked about

explanation.surface: A hat that people never stop talking about.
explanation.walkthrough: TOPIC loses its last letter. A topi is a sun helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: A pith helmet worn in hot countries.

parts.note: reads as a petticoat showing, but describes a blunder and, read as over plus sight, being on view

explanation.surface: Someone's underskirt is showing: how careless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slip' is a mistake, not an undergarment.
explanation.definitionFit: An unintentional omission or error caused by not noticing.

clue.text: They rush into house Ted has renovated

indicators.note: renovated means the words Ted has are done up into a new order

explanation.surface: People hurrying into a home that Ted has done up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They rush' is the definition, not a description of movers; 'renovated' rearranges Ted's two words, and 'into' merely joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Impetuous people act rashly and rush in.

clue.text: Good feeling if head of board left this plant

indicators.note: left here means left inside, so one piece is placed within the other
head of means the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Elation at a plant left by the board's chairman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head of' gives B from board; 'left' puts it into EUPHORIA. The plant is the spurge family.
explanation.definitionFit: Spurges such as poinsettia belong to this genus.

indicators.note: conditioned means the letters are treated and put into a new state

explanation.surface: Asking if a climbing plant was cooled by air-conditioning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conditioned' signals an anagram of WAS IT AIR; this spelling is a variant of wisteria.
explanation.definitionFit: A climbing plant with hanging lilac flowers.

indicators.note: construction of means the word semilune is built anew from its letters

explanation.surface: A chemical element found in a half-moon shaped construction.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-metallic chemical element, number 34.

clue.text: Philip is almost centrally placed here in Italy

indicators.note: centrally placed means the letters sit inside the run of words

explanation.surface: Philip is almost in the middle of Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tuscan city, famous for its leaning tower.

clue.text: What a candle, say, will do to this moth ?

definitions.text: What a candle, say, will do to this moth ?

parts.words: What a candle, say, will do to this moth
parts.note: a flame scorches a moth, and the verb for that leads into the name of a moth genus

explanation.surface: A moth flying too close to a candle flame.
explanation.walkthrough: A candle will burn a moth; the burnet is a day-flying moth.
explanation.definitionFit: Burnet moths are red-spotted day-flying moths.

indicators.note: loosely means the letters are not held in their fixed order

explanation.surface: Sorting rats into rough groups.
explanation.definitionFit: To sort into kinds or categories.

parts.note: a racing dog seems meant, but a fast liner was nicknamed a greyhound of the sea

explanation.surface: Choosing a breed of racing dog for a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'ocean greyhound' was a fast passenger liner.
explanation.definitionFit: The open sea, and the word paired with greyhound for a swift liner.

clue.text: Does this point to serious derangement?

definitions.text: Does this point to serious derangement?

parts.note: N is north, a compass point

indicators.note: derangement means the word serious is thrown out of order

explanation.surface: Asking whether a symptom indicates real mental disorder.
explanation.walkthrough: N for north is a compass point; 'derangement' jumbles the next word, and the whole clue doubles as a description of the condition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mental disorder marked by anxiety, which a doctor might ask about.

parts.note: a line from Shelley's Prometheus Unbound with its last word missing, to be supplied

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shelley with its final word left off.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is 'Pinnacled dim in the intense inane'; inane here means empty space.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley uses the word as a noun for the void of space.

definitions.meaning: a pointed arch with an S-shaped curve
read as two words, a cry of surprise

explanation.definitionFit: An S-curved moulding or arch, and split as 'O, gee!' a cry of surprise.

parts.note: the craft used by the three men in Jerome K. Jerome's comic novel Three Men in a Boat

explanation.surface: How three famous fictional characters travelled.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerome's three men rowed up the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: A small boat propelled by oars.

clue.text: Ran back into nasty, ruined mine

indicators.note: into means one piece goes inside the other
ruined means the word nasty is wrecked into a new order
back means the word ran is read from end to start

explanation.surface: Someone ran back into a horrible derelict mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the first word round and 'ruined' wrecks the adjective; 'into' places the one inside the other. A stannary is a tin mine, as in Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: A tin-mining district or tin mine, from Latin stannum, tin.

parts.note: at Oxford a famous river is called the Isis, so the waterway takes that name in its upper reaches

explanation.surface: A river named in honour of an Egyptian goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isis is the name of the London river where it flows through Oxford; the goddess is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: England's best-known river, flowing through Oxford and London.
